**Read more:** [book §16.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#166-cleanup-and-hygiene)

### IOS-017: Sign-in callback uses a custom URL scheme

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** days

**Why it matters:** A custom URL scheme isn't tied to your app. When the redirect goes through the OS (a scheme in CFBundleURLTypes), another app that registers it can receive the authorization code. Even inside ASWebAuthenticationSession, any app can start a sign-in with your client ID and scheme and impersonate your app. A verified https callback ties the redirect to your associated domain.

**Fix:** Return to a verified https redirect: Universal Links (Associated Domains applinks:) and, on iOS 17.4+, ASWebAuthenticationSession with .https(host:path:). Keep PKCE and state either way.

**Verify:** Install a test app that registers the same scheme, start sign-in, and confirm the callback can't reach it once the https redirect is in place.

**IDs:** MASWE-0029 · MASVS-PLATFORM-1

**Read more:** [book §17.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#175-deep-links-and-the-verification-that-makes-them-safe)

### IOS-018: Insecure NSKeyedUnarchiver API

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** unarchiveObject(with:) and unarchiveTopLevelObjectWithData build whatever classes the archive names. If an attacker controls the bytes (a file, a deep link, a shared item), they choose which objects your app constructs.

**Fix:** Decode with Codable. If you must read NSKeyedArchiver data, use unarchivedObject(ofClass:from:) with an NSSecureCoding class.

**Verify:** Search the code for unarchiveObject(with and unarchiveTopLevelObjectWithData and confirm no match remains.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4 · MASTG-TEST-0386

**Read more:** [book §19.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#194-deserialization)

### IOS-019: App target has no privacy manifest

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1, MAS-P · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Apple expects a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy in your app that declares collected data, tracking domains, and the reason for each required-reason API (UserDefaults is one). App Store Connect rejects uploads that use these APIs without a declared reason.

**Fix:** Add a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy to the app target (File > New > File > App Privacy) and fill in what the app and its SDKs collect and why.

**Verify:** Archive the app, then in Xcode's Organizer choose Generate Privacy Report and confirm it lists your app's manifest.

**IDs:** MASWE-0073 · MASVS-PRIVACY-3

**Read more:** [book §18.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#183-transparency-and-control)

### IOS-020: Secret copied to the general pasteboard without localOnly

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Without .localOnly, a value on the general pasteboard can travel to the user's other Apple devices through Universal Clipboard, and other apps can read it until something replaces it.

**Fix:** Copy secrets only when the user asks, with setItems(_:options:) and the options .localOnly: true and an .expirationDate.

**Verify:** Copy the value in the app, then try pasting on a second device signed in to the same Apple Account, and confirm nothing arrives; wait past the expiration and confirm the pasteboard is empty.

**IDs:** MASWE-0030 · MASVS-PLATFORM-1 · MASTG-TEST-0276 · MASTG-TEST-0277 · MASTG-TEST-0278 · MASTG-TEST-0279 · MASTG-TEST-0280

**Read more:** [book §6.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#66-how-to-implement-it)

### IOS-021: Release build keeps symbols or testability

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** ENABLE_TESTABILITY = YES exports internal symbols and makes Xcode skip stripping; STRIP_INSTALLED_PRODUCT = NO, STRIP_SWIFT_SYMBOLS = NO or a partial STRIP_STYLE ship the symbol table. All hand a reverse engineer readable function and type names for free.

**Fix:** In every configuration your schemes archive, set ENABLE_TESTABILITY = NO, STRIP_INSTALLED_PRODUCT = YES, STRIP_SWIFT_SYMBOLS = YES and STRIP_STYLE = all for the app, and keep symbols in a separate dSYM (DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT = dwarf-with-dsym).

**Verify:** Archive the release build and run `nm -U` on the app binary: you should see few or no readable Swift or Objective-C symbol names.

**IDs:** MASTG-TEST-0219

**Read more:** [book §15.8](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#158-build-configuration-in-code)

### IOS-022: Debug tool pod or package ships in release builds

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** In-app debug tools such as FLEX, netfox, Wormholy or CocoaDebug show network traffic, the view tree, files and Keychain items to whoever holds the phone. Linked into Release, they ship to every user.

**Fix:** Add :configurations => ['Debug'] to the pod, or wrap the import and setup in #if DEBUG. Swift Package Manager can't limit a package to one configuration, so guard every use.

**Verify:** Archive the Release build and run `otool -L` and `nm` on the app binary: no FLEX, netfox, Wormholy or CocoaDebug symbols should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0063 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4

**Read more:** [book §14.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#141-the-cheap-things-which-you-should-simply-do)

### IOS-023: Web view file-origin rules turned off through key-value coding

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** allowFileAccessFromFileURLs and allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs are private WebKit preferences. Set through setValue(_:forKey:), they let a file:// page read other local files, or any web origin, and send them anywhere.

**Fix:** Remove the setValue calls. Load bundled pages with loadFileURL(_:allowingReadAccessTo:) scoped to one folder, or serve them through a WKURLSchemeHandler.

**Verify:** Load a bundled page that tries `fetch('file:///etc/hosts')` and confirm WebKit blocks it.

**IDs:** MASWE-0034 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0335 · MASTG-BEST-0033

**Read more:** [book §16.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#163-file-access-the-setting-nobody-remembers-changing)

### IOS-024: Release entitlements let a debugger attach

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** get-task-allow = true lets any debugger attach to the process and read or change memory, keys and tokens. Distribution signing never sets it; a hard-coded true in a release entitlements file does.

**Fix:** Delete get-task-allow from the entitlements file. Xcode adds it for development signing only.

**Verify:** Run `codesign -d --entitlements - MyApp.app` on the archived build and confirm get-task-allow is absent or false.

**IDs:** MASWE-0063 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4 · MASTG-TEST-0261

**Read more:** [book §15.8](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#158-build-configuration-in-code)

### IOS-025: Release configuration compiles DEBUG-only code

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** When a shipping configuration defines DEBUG, every #if DEBUG block (test servers, logging, bypass switches) compiles into the App Store build. It also hides those blocks from scanners that assume DEBUG is off in release.

**Fix:** Remove DEBUG from SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS, OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS and GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS in every configuration your schemes archive.

**Verify:** Run `xcodebuild -showBuildSettings -configuration Release` and confirm DEBUG isn't in SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS or GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS.

**IDs:** MASWE-0063 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4

**Read more:** [book §15.8](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#158-build-configuration-in-code)

### IOS-026: Advertising identifier read without App Tracking Transparency

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Since iOS 14.5 the IDFA may be read only after the user allows tracking in the ATT prompt, which needs a purpose string. Reading it without both breaks App Store rules and tracks people who never agreed.

**Fix:** Call ATTrackingManager.requestTrackingAuthorization before you read the IDFA, and add NSUserTrackingUsageDescription. Better, use identifierForVendor or a server-side ID.

**Verify:** Reset the simulator's privacy settings, launch the app, and confirm the ATT prompt appears before any request carries the IDFA.

**IDs:** MASWE-0068 · MASVS-PRIVACY-2

**Read more:** [book §18.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#182-identifiers-and-tracking)

### IOS-027: Required-reason API used without a declared reason

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** UserDefaults, file timestamps, system boot time, disk space and active keyboards can fingerprint a device. Apple requires each use to be declared with an approved reason in PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, and App Store Connect rejects uploads that don't.

**Fix:** Add an NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes entry for the category with an approved reason code, such as CA92.1 for UserDefaults or C617.1 for file timestamps.

**Verify:** Archive the app, generate the privacy report in Xcode's Organizer, and confirm the category is listed with your reason.

**IDs:** MASWE-0073 · MASVS-PRIVACY-3

**Read more:** [book §18.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#183-transparency-and-control)

### IOS-028: App Attest isn't integrated

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** days · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** Without App Attest, the server can't tell your genuine app from a repackaged copy, an emulator script or a bot replaying your API. DeviceCheck alone only flags devices, not the app.

**Fix:** Generate and attest a key once per install with DCAppAttestService, send an assertion with sensitive requests, and verify both on the server. In React Native, use @react-native-firebase/app-check with the App Attest provider, or react-native-device-attest.

**Verify:** Call a sensitive endpoint with curl using a valid session and confirm the server rejects it for a missing or invalid assertion.

**IDs:** MASWE-0056 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-2

**Read more:** [book §10.7](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/04-proving-who-is-calling.md#107-how-to-implement-it)

### IOS-029: LocalAuthentication accepts a recent unlock

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** touchIDAuthenticationAllowableReuseDuration above zero lets a device unlock from the last few seconds or minutes satisfy the check with no new prompt, so whoever picks up an unlocked phone passes it.

**Fix:** Leave touchIDAuthenticationAllowableReuseDuration at 0 for payments, transfers and other sensitive actions.

**Verify:** Unlock the device, open the sensitive action right away, and confirm Face ID or Touch ID is requested again.

**IDs:** MASWE-0020 · MASVS-AUTH-2

**Read more:** [book §11.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/04-proving-who-is-calling.md#114-fallbacks-and-the-tension-inside-them)

### IOS-030: App never hides its screen in the app switcher or recordings

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** iOS stores a snapshot of the last screen for the app switcher, and screen recording or mirroring shows everything live. Without an overlay, balances, messages or one-time codes stay visible there.

**Fix:** Cover sensitive views in sceneWillResignActive and remove the cover in sceneDidBecomeActive, and watch sceneCaptureState (iOS 17+) to hide content while the screen is recorded. In React Native, use expo-screen-capture or react-native-capture-protection, or cover the screen when AppState turns inactive.

**Verify:** Open a sensitive screen, swipe to the app switcher, and confirm the snapshot shows the cover; start a screen recording and confirm the content is hidden.

**IDs:** MASWE-0038 · MASVS-PLATFORM-3

**Read more:** [book §6.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#65-the-leaks-that-are-not-about-encryption)

### IOS-031: Web view can read a whole app container folder

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** loadFileURL(_:allowingReadAccessTo:) with Documents, Library or the home folder lets the page, and any script injected into it, read every file there: databases, caches and downloaded documents.

**Fix:** Grant read access only to the folder that holds the page, such as a subfolder of Bundle.main.resourceURL.

**Verify:** From the loaded page, try to fetch a file outside its folder (for example a database in Library) and confirm it fails.

**IDs:** MASWE-0034 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0333 · MASTG-BEST-0033

**Read more:** [book §16.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#163-file-access-the-setting-nobody-remembers-changing)

### IOS-032: Deep link URL is loaded into a web view

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Any app or web page can open your URL scheme or universal link. If the URL it carries goes straight into a WKWebView, an attacker's page runs inside your app, next to its bridges and cookies.

**Fix:** Parse the incoming URL, require https, and compare its host with an exact allowlist before loading it. Open anything else in Safari or SFSafariViewController.

**Verify:** Run `xcrun simctl openurl booted '<scheme>://open?url=https://evil.example'` and confirm the web view doesn't load evil.example.

**IDs:** MASWE-0035 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0332 · MASTG-BEST-0034

**Read more:** [book §16.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#164-loading-untrusted-content)

### IOS-033: Network.framework connection allows TLS below 1.2

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** ATS doesn't cover Network.framework or Secure Transport connections. Allowing TLS 1.0 or 1.1 there lets an attacker on the network force a protocol with known weaknesses.

**Fix:** Set the minimum to .TLSv12 (or .TLSv13) with sec_protocol_options_set_min_tls_protocol_version.

**Verify:** Point the connection at a test server that only offers TLS 1.1 (`openssl s_server -tls1_1`) and confirm the handshake fails.

**IDs:** MASWE-0026 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-TEST-0344 · MASTG-BEST-0043

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### IOS-034: Sensitive files sit in a Documents folder the Files app shows

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** UIFileSharingEnabled exposes Documents in Finder and the Files app. Tokens, databases or exports stored there can be copied off the device by anyone with the phone, and they go into computer backups.

**Fix:** Keep app data in Application Support (or Caches), exclude it from backup where it fits, and put only files the user should see in Documents.

**Verify:** Connect the device to a Mac, open it in Finder's Files tab, and confirm no database, token or export file is listed for the app.

**IDs:** MASWE-0002 · MASVS-STORAGE-1 · MASTG-TEST-0303 · MASTG-BEST-0024

**Read more:** [book §6.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#65-the-leaks-that-are-not-about-encryption)

### IOS-035: Secret written to a file in the App Group container

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** The App Group container is shared with every app and extension in the group and isn't Keychain-protected. A token written there as a file is as exposed as plain storage, and every member can read it.

**Fix:** Share secrets through a Keychain access group (kSecAttrAccessGroup) instead, and keep only non-secret data in the group container.

**Verify:** On a simulator, open the group container (`xcrun simctl get_app_container booted <bundle id> <group id>`) and confirm no file holds a token or password.

**IDs:** MASWE-0001 · MASVS-STORAGE-1 · MASTG-TEST-0388 · MASTG-BEST-0068

**Read more:** [book §17.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#176-the-other-channels-people-forget)

### IOS-036: App doesn't refuse third-party keyboards

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes · **Only for:** banking, identity · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** A third-party keyboard with Full Access can send everything typed into your app, including passwords and card numbers, to its developer. iOS disables custom keyboards only in secure text fields.

**Fix:** Implement application(_:shouldAllowExtensionPointIdentifier:) and return false for .keyboard. In React Native, add it to AppDelegate (bare app) or through a config plugin (Expo).

**Verify:** Install a third-party keyboard, open the app, and confirm only the system keyboard appears in every field.

**Other apps:** Refusing custom keyboards takes away the user's preferred keyboard everywhere in the app. It pays off where typed credentials and transaction details are the asset; secure text fields already use the system keyboard (§17.6).

**IDs:** MASWE-0031 · MASVS-PLATFORM-1 · MASTG-TEST-0389 · MASTG-BEST-0069

**Read more:** [book §17.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#176-the-other-channels-people-forget)

### IOS-037: Bundled keyboard extension requests Full Access

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** RequestsOpenAccess gives your keyboard network access and shared storage, so everything users type in any app could leave the device. Users must trust you with all their input.

**Fix:** Set RequestsOpenAccess to false unless a feature the user sees needs the network or shared storage.

**Verify:** Install the keyboard and confirm Settings doesn't offer an Allow Full Access switch for it.

**IDs:** MASWE-0066 · MASVS-PRIVACY-1 · MASTG-TEST-0390 · MASTG-BEST-0069

**Read more:** [book §17.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#176-the-other-channels-people-forget)

### IOS-038: Protected resource used without a usable purpose string

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** iOS shows the purpose string in the permission prompt. A missing key makes the request fail (or the app get rejected); an empty or placeholder text gives users no basis for an informed choice.

**Fix:** Add the Info.plist usage key with a specific sentence that names the feature, such as "Scan a check to deposit it."

**Verify:** Reset privacy settings, trigger the feature, and confirm the prompt shows your specific explanation.

**IDs:** MASWE-0066 · MASVS-PRIVACY-1 · MASTG-TEST-0360 · MASTG-BEST-0051

**Read more:** [book §18.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#181-permissions-ask-for-less-later-and-explain-why)

### IOS-039: Entitlement has no matching feature in code

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Every entitlement widens what the app may reach (HealthKit, App Groups, iCloud, NFC). One the code never uses only adds attack surface and invites App Review questions.

**Fix:** Remove the capability in Xcode's Signing & Capabilities tab, which also deletes the entitlement.

**Verify:** Run `codesign -d --entitlements - MyApp.app` on the archive and confirm the entitlement is gone.

**IDs:** MASWE-0066 · MASVS-PRIVACY-1 · MASTG-TEST-0362 · MASTG-BEST-0051

**Read more:** [book §18.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#181-permissions-ask-for-less-later-and-explain-why)

### IOS-040: Tracking domain isn't declared in the privacy manifest

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Apple requires apps that track to set NSPrivacyTracking and list tracking domains in NSPrivacyTrackingDomains. Undeclared, the list misleads users, and iOS can't block those hosts when tracking is denied.

**Fix:** Set NSPrivacyTracking to true and add every tracking domain you contact to NSPrivacyTrackingDomains, or stop calling the domain.

**Verify:** Archive the app, generate the privacy report in Xcode's Organizer, and confirm the domain appears under tracking domains.

**IDs:** MASWE-0074 · MASVS-PRIVACY-3 · MASTG-TEST-0281

**Read more:** [book §18.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#183-transparency-and-control)

### IOS-041: App Attest uses the development environment in a release build

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** With appattest-environment set to development, the shipped app requests development attestations, which your server must accept from Apple's sandbox. Any developer-signed copy of the app can then pass.

**Fix:** Set com.apple.developer.devicecheck.appattest-environment to production in the release entitlements.

**Verify:** Check the archived app with `codesign -d --entitlements -` and confirm the value is production.

**IDs:** MASWE-0056 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-2

**Read more:** [book §10.7](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/04-proving-who-is-calling.md#107-how-to-implement-it)

### IOS-042: XML parser resolves external entities

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** With external entities or DTD loading on, a crafted XML document can make the parser read local files or send requests to other hosts (XXE), and nested entities can exhaust memory.

**Fix:** Leave shouldResolveExternalEntities false (the default) and drop XML_PARSE_NOENT and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD from libxml2 options.

**Verify:** Feed the parser a document with `<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/hosts">` and confirm the entity stays unresolved.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

### IOS-043: Sensitive text field lets the keyboard learn what is typed

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** The keyboard learns words typed into fields that aren't secure and keep autocorrection on. A PIN, card number or password typed there can be saved in the keyboard's word list and offered as a suggestion later, to anyone using the phone.

**Fix:** Use isSecureTextEntry = true (SecureField in SwiftUI) for passwords and PINs. For other sensitive fields, set autocorrectionType = .no and spellCheckingType = .no, or .autocorrectionDisabled() in SwiftUI.

**Verify:** Type a test value into the field, then start typing it in Notes. Confirm the keyboard doesn't suggest it.

**IDs:** MASWE-0036 · MASVS-PLATFORM-3 · MASTG-TEST-0313 · MASTG-DEMO-0076

**Read more:** [book §6.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#65-the-leaks-that-are-not-about-encryption)

### IOS-044: Socket connection sends data without TLS

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** App Transport Security covers URLSession only. A Network.framework connection that uses plain TCP, or a BSD socket or stream to port 80, sends its data in cleartext. Anyone on the same network can read and change it.

**Fix:** Use TLS for the connection: NWParameters(tls:) or .tls for Network.framework, or URLSession for HTTP. Keep plain TCP only for devices on the local network.

**Verify:** Capture the app's traffic with a proxy or packet capture and confirm this connection is TLS, not readable text.

**IDs:** MASWE-0026 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-TEST-0323

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### IOS-045: Password field rendered inside a web view

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A password typed into an HTML input lives in the page's DOM. Any script that runs in the web view, including an injected one, can read it there.

**Fix:** Collect passwords and other secrets with native views (a UITextField with isSecureTextEntry, or a SwiftUI SecureField) placed over the web view, and pass them to your code, not to the page.

**Verify:** Search the HTML the app loads for type="password" and confirm none is left.

**IDs:** MASTG-TEST-0378 · MASTG-BEST-0060

**Read more:** [book §16.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#165-sensitive-ui-inside-a-webview)

### IOS-046: Secret file is written where backups copy it

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Files in Documents and Library go into iCloud and computer backups unless they are excluded. A token, key or password file then leaves the device, and it can come back on a different phone.

**Fix:** Keep secrets in the Keychain with a ThisDeviceOnly class. If a file must hold one, set isExcludedFromBackup = true on the file's URLResourceValues after you write it.

**Verify:** Make an unencrypted computer backup of a test device and confirm the file isn't in it.

**IDs:** MASWE-0006 · MASVS-STORAGE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0215

**Read more:** [book §6.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#65-the-leaks-that-are-not-about-encryption)

### IOS-047: A host the app calls isn't in NSPinnedDomains

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours · **Only for:** banking, identity, health, ecommerce-cards

**Why it matters:** NSPinnedDomains pins only the hosts it lists, and NSIncludesSubdomains covers one subdomain level. Requests to any other host accept every publicly trusted certificate, so an attacker with a wrongly issued certificate for that host can read them.

**Fix:** Add every host that carries user data or tokens to NSPinnedDomains, with a backup pin. List deeper subdomains on their own. If a host is deliberately unpinned, write down why.

**Verify:** Run the app through a proxy whose CA the test device trusts, and confirm requests to this host fail.

**Other apps:** Book §8.8: outside banking, health, identity, and apps that handle card numbers, strict TLS plus Certificate Transparency monitoring is a reasonable position, and pinning adds operational risk.

**IDs:** MASWE-0028 · MASVS-NETWORK-2 · MASTG-TEST-0385

**Read more:** [book §8.10](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#810-how-to-implement-it)

## Kotlin Multiplatform

### KMP-001: Shared declaration is named after one platform's key mechanism

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A shared API such as `getKeystoreKey` forces Android's model onto iOS. The Secure Enclave holds only asymmetric keys, so the iOS implementation quietly weakens to fit the interface.

**Fix:** Name shared `expect` declarations and interfaces after the intent, such as `storeToken(token, requiringUserAuth)`, and let each platform's `actual` pick the right primitive. Prefer an interface with injected implementations to `expect class`, which is still Beta.

**Verify:** List every `expect` declaration and shared interface that touches keys or tokens; each name should describe what the caller needs, not a platform API.

**Read more:** [book §21.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#212-the-mistake-that-will-bite-you)

### KMP-002: Platform crypto, keystore, or biometric API used in commonMain

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Keystore and Keychain access, biometrics, and attestation get their security from one platform's hardware or vendor service. Shared code that reaches for them either fails to build for the other platform or hides a weaker fallback there.

**Fix:** Keep these calls in `androidMain` and `iosMain`. Put an intent-based interface in `commonMain` and inject each platform's implementation.

**Verify:** Search `commonMain` for `javax.crypto`, `java.security`, `android.security`, `androidx.biometric`, `platform.Security`, and `platform.LocalAuthentication`; nothing should remain.

**Read more:** [book §21.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#211-the-line-and-the-reasoning-behind-it)

### KMP-003: Ktor pins are shared, but an engine doesn't enforce them

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Ktor's common API doesn't pin; each engine enforces pins separately. A project that configures Android and forgets iOS is pinned on one platform and open on the other, and its tests still pass.

**Fix:** Keep the pin strings in `commonMain`, and enforce them in each platform's `actual`: OkHttp's `CertificatePinner` on Android and the Darwin engine's `CertificatePinner` through `handleChallenge` on iOS. Put both in the same pull request.

**Verify:** Put a proxy such as mitmproxy in front of the app and make the device trust its CA (§8.10, Verify it). Requests to the pinned host should fail on Android and on iOS.

**IDs:** MASWE-0028 · MASVS-NETWORK-2

**Read more:** [book §8.10](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#810-how-to-implement-it)

### KMP-004: Ktor client logs headers or bodies in every build

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Ktor's Logging plugin at `HEADERS`, `BODY`, or `ALL` writes the `Authorization` header or login responses to logcat and the iOS console in release builds too, unless headers are sanitized or the level depends on a debug flag.

**Fix:** Use `LogLevel.NONE` in release builds, and add `sanitizeHeader { it == HttpHeaders.Authorization }` wherever headers are logged.

**Verify:** Install a release build, sign in, and watch `adb logcat` or Console.app: no `Authorization` header or response body should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0005 · MASVS-STORAGE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0231 · MASTG-TEST-0297

**Read more:** [book §6.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#66-how-to-implement-it)

### KMP-005: Kotlin iOS code accepts any server certificate

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Answering the server-trust challenge with `NSURLCredential` for the presented trust, without evaluating it first, accepts any certificate. Anyone on the network can then read and change the app's traffic on iOS.

**Fix:** Call `SecTrustEvaluateWithError` on `challenge.protectionSpace.serverTrust` and cancel the challenge when it fails, or use Ktor's Darwin `CertificatePinner`, which validates the chain first.

**Verify:** Route an iPhone through a proxy whose CA it doesn't trust; every request from the shared client should fail.

**IDs:** MASWE-0027 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-TEST-0396

**Read more:** [book §8.10](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#810-how-to-implement-it)

### KMP-006: Shared settings library stores a token in plain storage

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** multiplatform-settings writes to SharedPreferences on Android and NSUserDefaults on iOS. Both are plain files that backups copy, so a token or password stored there can be read and replayed.

**Fix:** Put secrets behind an `expect` interface backed by `KeychainSettings` on Apple and a Keystore-backed store (Tink with DataStore) on Android. Keep only non-secret settings in plain storage.

**Verify:** Sign in on an emulator and run `adb shell run-as <package> cat shared_prefs/*.xml`; no token or password should appear. On iOS, check the app's Preferences plist the same way.

**IDs:** MASWE-0001 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §21.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#212-the-mistake-that-will-bite-you)

## Flutter

### FLT-001: Dart badCertificateCallback accepts every certificate

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A `badCertificateCallback` that returns `true` turns off TLS server checks for Dart's HttpClient, and for Dio or package:http clients built on it. Anyone on the same network can impersonate your server and read or change the traffic.

**Fix:** Delete the callback, or return `false` from it. For a local test server, trust its certificate in a debug-only `SecurityContext` instead. If you need pinning, use `SecurityContext(withTrustedRoots: false)` with your CA's certificate, which keeps the normal checks.

**Verify:** Send the app's traffic through a proxy whose CA the phone doesn't trust and confirm every request fails with a HandshakeException.

**IDs:** MASWE-0027 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-KNOW-0015

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### FLT-002: Token or password stored in shared_preferences

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** shared_preferences writes a plain XML file on Android and a UserDefaults plist on iOS. Both are copied into backups and are readable by anyone with access to the device's files, so a long-lived token there can be lifted and replayed.

**Fix:** Keep short-lived tokens in memory. Store long-lived tokens and credentials with `flutter_secure_storage`, which uses the Android Keystore and the iOS Keychain, and set `IOSOptions(accessibility: KeychainAccessibility.first_unlock_this_device)` or stricter. Leave only non-secret settings in shared_preferences.

**Verify:** Sign in on an emulator, then run `adb shell run-as <package> cat shared_prefs/FlutterSharedPreferences.xml` and confirm no token or password appears.

**IDs:** MASWE-0001 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §6.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#64-the-uncomfortable-question-nobody-asked)

### FLT-003: Dio logger prints headers or bodies in release builds

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** PrettyDioLogger, and a LogInterceptor with a custom `logPrint` (or on dio 4), print every request with `print`, which reaches logcat and the device console in release builds. The `Authorization` header and login responses end up in logs and bug reports.

**Fix:** Add logging interceptors only under `if (kDebugMode)`, and redact the `Authorization` and cookie headers in any logger that stays.

**Verify:** Install a release build, sign in, and watch `adb logcat` or Console.app: no request headers, tokens, or response bodies should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0005 · MASVS-STORAGE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0231 · MASTG-TEST-0297

**Read more:** [book §6.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#66-how-to-implement-it)

### FLT-004: Flutter web view can read local files or load mixed content

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** With file-origin access on, a page loaded from a file can read other local files, such as the app's databases, and send them anywhere. Allowing mixed content lets an HTTPS page pull scripts over plain HTTP that anyone on the network can replace.

**Fix:** Remove these flutter_inappwebview settings. Serve bundled HTML through `webViewAssetLoader` over `https://appassets.androidplatform.net` instead of `file://` URLs.

**Verify:** Search for `allowFileAccessFromFileURLs`, `allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs`, `allowFileAccess: true`, and `MIXED_CONTENT_ALWAYS_ALLOW`; none should remain.

**IDs:** MASWE-0034 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0252 · MASTG-TEST-0335

**Read more:** [book §16.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#163-file-access-the-setting-nobody-remembers-changing)

### FLT-005: Flutter web view accepts any server certificate

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A trust handler that answers PROCEED without checking the certificate turns off TLS for the web view. Anyone on the same network can serve their own page with a self-signed certificate and read or change what the user sees and types.

**Fix:** Delete the handler so the platform validates the chain, or return `CANCEL` unless your own pin check on the server certificate passes.

**Verify:** Route the device through a proxy whose CA it doesn't trust; the web view should refuse to load the page.

**IDs:** MASWE-0027 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-TEST-0284 · MASTG-TEST-0397

**Read more:** [book §16.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#164-loading-untrusted-content)

### FLT-006: Flutter web view debugging is on in release

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** With web contents debugging or `isInspectable` on, anyone holding the device can attach Chrome DevTools or Safari's Web Inspector, read cookies and tokens from the page, and run their own script in it.

**Fix:** Pass `kDebugMode` instead of `true`, so debugging is on only in debug builds.

**Verify:** Install a release build and open `chrome://inspect` (or Safari's Develop menu); the app's web view should not be listed.

**IDs:** MASWE-0063 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4 · MASTG-TEST-0227 · MASTG-BEST-0008

**Read more:** [book §16.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#166-cleanup-and-hygiene)

### FLT-007: Flutter biometric check only returns a boolean

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** days

**Why it matters:** local_auth's `authenticate()` returns true or false and unlocks nothing. On a rooted or jailbroken device a hook makes it return true, and since no key needed the biometric, the protected data opens anyway.

**Fix:** Keep the secret under a key that only biometric authentication unlocks, with `biometric_storage` or a platform channel to a Keystore key with a CryptoObject or a Keychain item with `SecAccessControl`. Don't gate on the boolean.

**Verify:** Hook `authenticate` to return true with Frida (`frida -U -f <app>`); the protected data should still stay locked because no key was released.

**IDs:** MASWE-0020 · MASVS-AUTH-2 · MASTG-TEST-0266 · MASTG-TEST-0327 · MASTG-BEST-0036

**Read more:** [book §11.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/04-proving-who-is-calling.md#111-decorative-versus-real)

### FLT-008: Flutter release build is not obfuscated

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Without `--obfuscate`, the compiled Dart code keeps its class and function names, so tools such as blutter map the app's logic, including its integrity and root checks, in minutes.

**Fix:** Add `--obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols` to every release `flutter build` command, and keep the symbol files to decode crash reports.

**Verify:** Run `strings` on `libapp.so` from the release APK and confirm your own class names, such as your login screen's, no longer appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0059 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-3 · MASTG-TEST-0368

**Read more:** [book §14.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#143-where-obfuscation-genuinely-helps)

## React Native

### RN-001: Token or password stored in AsyncStorage, unencrypted MMKV, or redux-persist

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** AsyncStorage and MMKV without an `encryptionKey` write plain files in the app's private folder, and redux-persist saves through them. These files are copied into backups and are readable by anyone with access to the device's files, so a long-lived token there can be lifted and replayed.

**Fix:** Keep short-lived tokens in memory. Store long-lived tokens and passwords with react-native-keychain or expo-secure-store, which use the Android Keystore and the iOS Keychain. For MMKV, pass an `encryptionKey` that you generate once and keep in the Keychain or Keystore. For redux-persist, leave the auth slice out of `whitelist` or persist it through encrypted storage.

**Verify:** Sign in on an emulator, then run `adb shell run-as <package> ls -R databases files` and print the storage files (AsyncStorage uses `databases/RKStorage`, MMKV uses `files/mmkv`). Confirm no token or password appears in readable form.

**IDs:** MASWE-0001 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §6.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#64-the-uncomfortable-question-nobody-asked)

### RN-002: Secret bundled into the app through build-time config

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** react-native-config, `EXPO_PUBLIC_` variables, react-native-dotenv, and Expo's `extra` copy their values into the app when it is built. Anyone who downloads the app can read them, so a secret placed there can be used against your accounts.

**Fix:** Rotate the secret first, because it has already shipped. Then move the call that needs it behind your backend. Keep build-only secrets in EAS environment variables with secret visibility or in your CI secret store, without the `EXPO_PUBLIC_` prefix, and don't copy them into `extra`. Public client identifiers, such as a Sentry DSN or a Firebase web `apiKey`, may stay.

**Verify:** Build a release, unzip the APK or IPA, and search the JavaScript bundle (`index.android.bundle` or `main.jsbundle`), `BuildConfig`, and `Info.plist` for the secret's value. Nothing should come back.

**IDs:** MASWE-0004 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §15.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#152-secrets-classify-then-protect)

### RN-003: HTTP requests or responses are logged in every build

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** An axios interceptor that prints headers or bodies, redux-logger, and react-native-network-logger also run in release builds unless you guard them. The `Authorization` header, tokens, and API responses then reach the device log, bug reports, or an in-app screen.

**Fix:** Add logging interceptors, redux-logger, and `startNetworkLogging()` only under `if (__DEV__)`. Log the method, URL, and status, never headers or bodies. Remove console calls from release builds with babel-plugin-transform-remove-console.

**Verify:** Install a release build, sign in, and watch `adb logcat` or Console.app: no request headers, tokens, or response bodies should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0005 · MASVS-STORAGE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0231 · MASTG-TEST-0297

**Read more:** [book §6.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#66-how-to-implement-it)

### RN-004: JS networking library accepts any server certificate

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** `disableAllSecurity: true` in react-native-ssl-pinning and `trusty: true` in rn-fetch-blob or react-native-blob-util turn off certificate checks for those requests. Anyone on the same network can impersonate your server and read or change the traffic.

**Fix:** Remove the option, or set it to `false`. For a local test server, trust its certificate in a debug-only network security config on Android or a debug-only trust setting on iOS. To pin certificates, pass `sslPinning: { certs: [...] }` to react-native-ssl-pinning, which keeps the normal checks.

**Verify:** Send the app's traffic through a proxy whose CA the phone doesn't trust, and confirm these requests fail.

**IDs:** MASWE-0027 · MASVS-NETWORK-1

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### RN-005: WebView can read local files

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** With file access on, a page in the WebView can open file:// URLs. With file-URL access also on, a script in a file:// page can read the app's private files and send them to a server.

**Fix:** Remove `allowFileAccess`, `allowFileAccessFromFileURLs` and `allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs`. They are off by default. Pass bundled HTML with `source={{ html }}` or `require()`. On iOS, point `allowingReadAccessToURL` at the one folder that holds the page.

**Verify:** Load a page that runs `fetch('file:///data/data/<your.package>/shared_prefs/')` and confirm the request fails.

**IDs:** MASWE-0034 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0250 · MASTG-TEST-0252 · MASTG-TEST-0253

**Read more:** [book §16.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#163-file-access-the-setting-nobody-remembers-changing)

### RN-006: WebView may navigate to any origin or URL scheme

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** `originWhitelist={['*']}` lets the WebView itself open every URL it is sent to, in any scheme. A link, a redirect, or a script on a remote page can then load file://, data: or an attacker's site inside your app.

**Fix:** Remove `originWhitelist` to keep the default (http and https), or list the exact origins you own, such as `['https://app.example.com']`. Keep `['*']` only for a WebView that shows your own HTML string.

**Verify:** From the page, navigate to a URL outside the list and confirm the WebView doesn't load it inside the app.

**IDs:** MASWE-0035 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0398

**Read more:** [book §16.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#164-loading-untrusted-content)

### RN-007: WebView loads a URL from navigation params or user input with no allowlist

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** The WebView loads whatever URL a screen receives in its params, or whatever the user types. A deep link or another app can then choose the page that runs inside your app, next to its bridge and cookies.

**Fix:** Parse the URL with `new URL()`, require https, and compare the hostname with an exact allowlist before you render the WebView. Run the same check in `onShouldStartLoadWithRequest`.

**Verify:** Open the screen with `https://evil.example/` as its URL param and confirm the WebView refuses it.

**IDs:** MASWE-0035 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0398 · MASTG-TEST-0332

**Read more:** [book §16.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#164-loading-untrusted-content)

### RN-008: WebView bridge trusts the page

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** An `onMessage` handler that acts on every message lets any page the WebView reaches, or an iframe inside it, call your app code. A value placed in an injected script without encoding can run its own JavaScript in the page.

**Fix:** In `onMessage`, check `new URL(event.nativeEvent.url).origin` against your origin, then validate the message. Send data to the page with `postMessage`, or encode it with `JSON.stringify` before you put it in a script.

**Verify:** Load a page from another origin, call `window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(...)` from it, and confirm the app ignores the message.

**IDs:** MASWE-0033 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0334 · MASTG-TEST-0376

**Read more:** [book §16.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#162-the-javascript-bridge-and-why-its-the-sharpest-edge)

### RN-009: Deep-link data reaches openURL, fetch, a WebView, or navigation without an allowlist

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Anyone can send the user a link to your app, so every part of a deep link is attacker input. If the link's URL or a query value is opened with `Linking.openURL`, fetched, loaded in a WebView, or handed to a screen as a URL, the attacker picks the destination.

**Fix:** Parse the link with `new URL()` and compare `protocol` and `hostname` to a fixed allowlist before using it. Map link paths to screen names and plain IDs, never to raw URLs.

**Verify:** Open `myapp://open?next=https://evil.example` (or `adb shell am start -d '<link>'` on Android). The app should refuse it and stay on a safe screen.

**IDs:** MASWE-0029 · MASVS-PLATFORM-1 · MASTG-BEST-0071 · MASTG-TEST-0394 · MASTG-TEST-0395

**Read more:** [book §17.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#175-deep-links-and-the-verification-that-makes-them-safe)

### RN-010: JavaScript code is built from a string at runtime

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** `eval`, `new Function`, and `setTimeout` with a string run text as code. If any part of that text comes from a server, a deep link, a WebView message, or storage, an attacker's text runs with everything the app can reach.

**Fix:** Remove the runtime code. Parse data with `JSON.parse`, pick behavior from a fixed map of functions, and pass functions, not strings, to `setTimeout` and `setInterval`.

**Verify:** Search the app's own code for `eval(`, `Function(`, and `setTimeout(` with a string. No call should take text that is built at runtime.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

### RN-011: SQLite query built by joining strings

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** When a value is pasted into the SQL text, a quote in that value changes the query. An attacker who controls a search term, a message, or a deep-link value can read or delete other rows in the local database.

**Fix:** Write `?` placeholders in the SQL and pass the values in the parameters array (`executeSql(sql, [a, b])`, `runAsync(sql, a, b)`). Pick table, column, and sort names from a fixed list.

**Verify:** Pass a value such as `' OR '1'='1` through the code path and confirm the query treats it as plain text.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4 · MASTG-TEST-0339

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

### RN-012: React Native biometric check only returns a boolean

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** days

**Why it matters:** `authenticateAsync()`, `simplePrompt()`, and similar calls return success or failure and unlock nothing. On a rooted or jailbroken device a hook makes them return success, and since no key needed the biometric, the protected data opens anyway.

**Fix:** Keep the secret in an item that only biometric authentication releases: react-native-keychain with `accessControl: ACCESS_CONTROL.BIOMETRY_CURRENT_SET`, or expo-secure-store with `requireAuthentication: true`. Or sign a server challenge with react-native-biometrics `createSignature`.

**Verify:** Hook the prompt to return success with Frida (`frida -U -f <app>`). The protected data should stay locked, because no key was released.

**IDs:** MASWE-0020 · MASVS-AUTH-2 · MASTG-TEST-0266 · MASTG-TEST-0327 · MASTG-BEST-0036

**Read more:** [book §11.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/04-proving-who-is-calling.md#111-decorative-versus-real)

### RN-013: crypto-js derives the AES key from a passphrase string

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** When `CryptoJS.AES.encrypt` gets a string key, crypto-js treats it as a passphrase. It makes the real key and IV with one round of MD5 (OpenSSL EVP_BytesToKey), so an attacker who copies the data can test billions of guesses per second.

**Fix:** Pass a random 256-bit key as a WordArray, kept in the Keychain or Keystore (for example through react-native-keychain), with a random IV for each message. Better, use native AES-GCM. If the key must come from a password, use PBKDF2 with SHA-256 and at least 600,000 iterations.

**Verify:** Search for `AES.encrypt(` and `AES.decrypt(`. Each call should get a WordArray key and an `iv` option, never a string.

**IDs:** MASWE-0014 · MASVS-CRYPTO-2

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### RN-014: Over-the-air JavaScript updates are not signature-checked

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** expo-updates and CodePush replace the app's JavaScript after install. Without code signing, the app runs whatever bundle the update server sends, so anyone who controls that server, its account, or the network path controls the app.

**Fix:** For expo-updates, generate a key pair with `npx expo-updates codesigning:generate`, then set `updates.codeSigningCertificate` and `updates.codeSigningMetadata` and sign each update. For CodePush, release with a private key and add `CodePushPublicKey` to Info.plist and strings.xml.

**Verify:** Publish an update without the signature (or with a different key) to a test channel, and confirm the app refuses it and keeps running the embedded bundle.

**IDs:** MASWE-0049 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#195-dynamic-code-loading)

### RN-015: JavaScript console output ships in release builds

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** React Native release builds keep every `console.log`, and send it to logcat on Android and the system log on iOS. A logged token, email, or API response is readable over adb, in bug reports, and by crash tools that collect recent log lines.

**Fix:** Add `babel-plugin-transform-remove-console` to the production env of your babel config (keep `error` and `warn` if you need them), or set metro's `minifierConfig.compress.drop_console` to true. Wrap the remaining debug logging in `if (__DEV__)`.

**Verify:** Build a release bundle with `npx react-native bundle --dev false` (or `npx expo export`), and confirm `grep -c console.log` on the output finds none of your own log lines.

**IDs:** MASWE-0005 · MASVS-STORAGE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0231 · MASTG-BEST-0002

**Read more:** [book §6.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#66-how-to-implement-it)

### RN-016: Hermes is turned off

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** With Hermes off, the app ships its JavaScript as a readable text bundle. Anyone who unzips the app can read, search, and edit the logic, including root and integrity checks. Hermes ships compiled bytecode, which costs more to read and change.

**Fix:** Turn Hermes back on: `hermesEnabled=true` in android/gradle.properties, remove `:hermes_enabled => false` from the Podfile, and remove `"jsEngine": "jsc"` from app.json. Hermes is the default since React Native 0.70.

**Verify:** Unzip the release APK and run `xxd -l 4 assets/index.android.bundle`: a Hermes bundle starts with the bytes `c61f bc03`, while a JavaScript bundle starts with readable text.

**IDs:** MASWE-0059 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-3

**Read more:** [book §14.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#143-where-obfuscation-genuinely-helps)

### RN-017: JavaScript source map ships inside the app

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A source map turns the minified bundle back into the original file names, function names, and code layout. Packaged in the app, it gives anyone who unzips it your readable source.

**Fix:** Write source maps to the build folder, upload them to your crash reporter (Sentry, Bugsnag) from CI, and keep them out of the app's assets and Xcode resources.

**Verify:** Run `unzip -l app-release.apk | grep '\.map'` and list the .ipa's app folder: no `.map` file should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0061 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-3

**Read more:** [book §15.8](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#158-build-configuration-in-code)

### RN-018: Debug tooling connects in release builds

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Reactotron, Flipper plugins, and remote Redux DevTools stream app state, network calls, and storage to a desktop tool. Started outside `__DEV__`, they run in the store build and send that data to whatever host they are set to.

**Fix:** Start the tool only inside `if (__DEV__) { ... }`, and load its config file with `if (__DEV__) require('./ReactotronConfig')`. Keep `developmentClient: true` out of store build profiles in eas.json.

**Verify:** Build a release bundle and search it for `reactotron`, `flipper`, and `remotedev`: none should be found, and the app should open no connection to port 9090 or 8000.

**IDs:** MASWE-0063 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4 · MASTG-BEST-0007

**Read more:** [book §14.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#141-the-cheap-things-which-you-should-simply-do)

### RN-019: npm dependencies can be swapped at the source or in transit

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A dependency taken from a git branch or tag, a plain-HTTP address, or `*` can change with no change to your code. A registry over HTTP or with TLS checks off lets anyone on the network swap packages, and a committed registry token lets anyone with the repository publish as you.

**Fix:** Pin git dependencies to a full commit SHA, or publish them to a registry. Use version ranges with a committed lockfile. Use an https registry, keep `strict-ssl` and `enableStrictSsl` on, and read registry tokens from the environment, for example `_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}`.

**Verify:** Check that every git dependency in package.json ends in `#` and a 40-character commit SHA, and that .npmrc and .yarnrc.yml have no `http://` registry, no `false` TLS setting, and no literal token. Then run `npm ci` or `yarn install --immutable` on a clean checkout.

**Read more:** [book §15.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#154-dependencies-and-build-inputs)

### RN-020: Native module runs a shell command or opens a file path sent from JavaScript

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Every JavaScript file in the app can call a native module method. If the method passes its argument to a shell or opens it as a file path, any script that runs in the app (a WebView injection or a bad update) can run commands or read the app's private files.

**Fix:** Remove generic `exec` and `readFile` bridge methods. Expose only the specific action the app needs, take a name from a fixed list instead of a path, and check that the resolved canonical path stays inside the app's folder.

**Verify:** Call the method from JavaScript with `../../databases/app.db` or `id; ls`. It should refuse both.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

## Cross-platform code

### XPL-001: Restricted or server-only secret is hardcoded in the app

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Anything in the app can be extracted by anyone who downloads it. A cloud key, model-provider key, payment key, repository token, or private key found this way lets an attacker spend your money or act as your servers.

**Fix:** Rotate the credential first, because it is already exposed. Then move the call behind your backend so the key never ships, and read server-side keys from your CI or server secret store.

**Verify:** Run `strings` on the release APK or IPA and search for the key's prefix; nothing should come back. Turn on push protection or a secret scanner so a new key can't be committed.

**IDs:** MASWE-0004 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §15.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#152-secrets-classify-then-protect)

### XPL-002: Google API key in code (restrict it in the console)

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Maps and Firebase keys are client identifiers: they ship in every app and anyone can read them. Without restrictions, someone else can use your key and your quota.

**Fix:** In Google Cloud Console, restrict the key to your Android package name and signing certificate, or your iOS bundle ID, and to only the APIs it needs. If it calls a paid API such as Gemini, move that call behind your backend instead.

**Verify:** In Google Cloud Console, open the key's page and confirm it lists application restrictions and API restrictions.

**Read more:** [book §15.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#152-secrets-classify-then-protect)

### XPL-003: Client or API secret is assigned a literal value

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A value named as a secret ships inside the app, where anyone can extract it. An OAuth client secret in a mobile app protects nothing and lets others impersonate your app to the server.

**Fix:** Rotate the secret. Mobile OAuth clients should use PKCE with no client secret; other secrets belong on your backend. If the value is not a secret, rename it so reviewers can tell.

**Verify:** Search the release build with `strings` for the value; it should be gone.

**IDs:** MASWE-0004 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §15.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#152-secrets-classify-then-protect)

### XPL-004: AES in ECB mode, or with no mode named

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** ECB encrypts identical blocks to identical ciphertext, so patterns in the data show through, and it detects no tampering. On Android, `Cipher.getInstance("AES")` with no mode can silently give you ECB.

**Fix:** Use AES-GCM (`AES/GCM/NoPadding`) with a Keystore key, or Tink's AEAD, or CryptoKit's `AES.GCM` on iOS. Re-encrypt existing data under the new scheme.

**Verify:** Search for `AES/ECB`, `"AES"`, and `kCCOptionECBMode`; every remaining hit should be gone or explained in a comment.

**IDs:** MASWE-0007 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1 · MASTG-TEST-0232 · MASTG-TEST-0350 · MASTG-TEST-0317

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-005: AES-CBC needs a separate MAC to detect tampering

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** CBC hides data but doesn't detect changes. An attacker can alter ciphertext to change the plaintext predictably, and padding errors can leak the plaintext byte by byte.

**Fix:** Prefer AES-GCM. If you must keep CBC, compute an HMAC-SHA-256 over the IV and the ciphertext with a separate key, and check it in constant time before decrypting.

**Verify:** For each hit, confirm a MAC over IV plus ciphertext is checked before decryption, or that the code moved to GCM.

**IDs:** MASWE-0007 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-006: Fixed IV or nonce

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** An IV or nonce must be fresh for every message. With GCM, one repeat under the same key reveals the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker forge messages.

**Fix:** Don't supply an IV. Let the Keystore, Tink, or CryptoKit generate a random 12-byte nonce for each encryption, and store it next to the ciphertext.

**Verify:** For each encryption call, confirm the IV comes from `cipher.iv` after `init`, or from a secure random source, never from a constant.

**IDs:** MASWE-0007 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-007: MD5 or SHA-1 used to protect a password, signature, or token

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Attackers can build two different inputs with the same MD5 or SHA-1 hash, and both are fast to brute-force. Code that relies on them for passwords, signatures, or integrity can be forged or cracked.

**Fix:** Use SHA-256 or stronger. If the hash is only a non-security checksum, such as detecting a corrupted download, add a comment saying so.

**Verify:** For each hit, confirm it now uses SHA-256 or stronger, or a password hash such as Argon2id for passwords.

**IDs:** MASWE-0008 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1 · MASTG-TEST-0211

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-008: Non-cryptographic or seeded random number generator

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Default random generators are built for speed, not unpredictability: an attacker can often predict later values from a few samples. A seeded generator repeats its values for anyone who can guess the seed.

**Fix:** For keys, nonces, salts, and tokens, use `SecureRandom()` with the default constructor on Android and `SecRandomCopyBytes` on iOS, and never seed them. Other uses, such as shuffling a list for display, are fine.

**Verify:** For each hit, confirm the value doesn't protect anything, or that it now comes from `SecureRandom` or `SecRandomCopyBytes`.

**IDs:** MASWE-0012 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1 · MASTG-TEST-0204 · MASTG-TEST-0205 · MASTG-TEST-0311 · MASTG-TEST-0349

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-009: Hardcoded plain-HTTP URL

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Anyone on the same network, such as public Wi-Fi, can read and change plain HTTP traffic. Even if the platform blocks cleartext today, an exception added later would let this URL through.

**Fix:** Change the URL to `https://`. If the server doesn't support HTTPS, fix the server; don't add a cleartext exception.

**Verify:** Build a release version and confirm requests to this host use HTTPS, or fail with a cleartext error.

**IDs:** MASWE-0026 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-TEST-0233 · MASTG-TEST-0321 · MASTG-TEST-0236

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### XPL-010: Token, password, or secret written to the log

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A token in a log line is a token on disk. Logs reach `adb logcat`, bug reports, and crash reporters that upload recent lines.

**Fix:** Remove the value from the message. Plant a release logging tree that drops everything below error, and strip `Log.v/d/i` with R8's `-assumenosideeffects`. On iOS, remove debug logging from release builds; where a log line stays, use `Logger` and leave dynamic values at the default `.private` privacy, never `privacy: .public` for a token.

**Verify:** Install a release build, sign in, and watch `adb logcat` (or Console.app on iOS): no token or password should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0005 · MASVS-STORAGE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0203 · MASTG-TEST-0231 · MASTG-TEST-0296 · MASTG-TEST-0297

**Read more:** [book §6.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#65-the-leaks-that-are-not-about-encryption)

### XPL-011: Encryption key is hardcoded in the app

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Anything in the app package is public. A key written in the code can be read from the APK or IPA in minutes, and then every copy of the encrypted data can be decrypted. It also can't be rotated without an app update.

**Fix:** Generate the key on the device inside the Android Keystore or the iOS Keychain or Secure Enclave, and never export it. Tink with a Keystore-protected keyset does this for you. If a server must decrypt, wrap a random per-session key with the server's public key instead of sharing one symmetric key.

**Verify:** For every `SecretKeySpec(`, `SymmetricKey(data:`, and `Key.from…(` call, confirm the key bytes come from the Keystore, the Keychain, Tink, or a secure random source, never from a string or byte literal.

**IDs:** MASWE-0003 · MASVS-STORAGE-1 · MASTG-TEST-0212 · MASTG-TEST-0213

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-012: Secret copied to the clipboard without the sensitive flag

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Any app that reads the clipboard, and the keyboard, can see a copied password, code, or token. Android 13 and later show the copied text in a preview unless the clip is marked sensitive.

**Fix:** Don't copy secrets. If the user asks to copy one, set `ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE` in the clip's extras (API 33+) and clear the clip after a short timeout.

**Verify:** Copy the value on an Android 13 device and confirm the system preview shows dots instead of the text.

**IDs:** MASWE-0030 · MASVS-PLATFORM-1

**Read more:** [book §6.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#66-how-to-implement-it)

### XPL-013: Broken cipher (DES, 3DES, RC4, RC2, or Blowfish)

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** DES keys can be brute-forced, 3DES and Blowfish use 64-bit blocks that leak data after a few gigabytes (Sweet32), and RC4's output is biased. Data encrypted with them should be treated as readable.

**Fix:** Use AES-GCM through the Keystore, CryptoKit, or Tink. Re-encrypt stored legacy data with the new scheme the first time you read it.

**Verify:** Search for `DES`, `RC4`, `RC2`, `Blowfish`, and `kCCAlgorithm`; only AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 should remain.

**IDs:** MASWE-0007 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1 · MASTG-TEST-0221 · MASTG-TEST-0210 · MASTG-BEST-0009

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-014: Encryption key is too small

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** RSA, DSA, and DH keys below 2,048 bits, curves below 224 bits, and symmetric keys below 128 bits can be broken with today's hardware, which exposes everything they protect or sign.

**Fix:** Use P-256 (EC) keys generated in the Keystore or Secure Enclave. If you need RSA, use at least 2,048 bits, and 3,072 for keys that must last beyond 2030.

**Verify:** For each key generator, confirm the size is at least 2,048 bits for RSA, a curve of at least P-256, or at least 128 bits for AES.

**IDs:** MASWE-0013 · MASVS-CRYPTO-2 · MASTG-TEST-0208 · MASTG-TEST-0209

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-015: PBKDF2 uses too few iterations

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A password-derived key is only as strong as the work an attacker must repeat per guess. With few PBKDF2 iterations, a stolen salt and hash or ciphertext falls to a GPU dictionary attack in hours.

**Fix:** Prefer Argon2id. If PBKDF2 is required, use HMAC-SHA-256 with at least 600,000 iterations. For a short PIN, gate a Keystore or Secure Enclave key with user authentication instead.

**Verify:** Confirm the iteration count meets OWASP's minimum for the PRF: 600,000 for HMAC-SHA-256, 210,000 for HMAC-SHA-512, 1,300,000 for HMAC-SHA-1.

**IDs:** MASWE-0014 · MASVS-CRYPTO-2

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-016: Password hashing uses a fixed salt

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A salt written in the code is the same for every user and install, so one precomputed table or one GPU run attacks every derived key at once, and equal passwords give equal keys.

**Fix:** Generate a random 16-byte salt per secret with `SecureRandom` or `SecRandomCopyBytes`, and store it next to the derived data.

**Verify:** For each PBKDF2 call, confirm the salt comes from a secure random source or from storage, never from a literal.

**IDs:** MASWE-0014 · MASVS-CRYPTO-2

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-017: gRPC channel sends traffic in plain text

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A plaintext gRPC channel skips TLS entirely, and Network Security Config and ATS don't cover gRPC sockets. Anyone on the network can read and change every call, including auth metadata.

**Fix:** Use `useTransportSecurity()` (grpc-java), `.tls` (grpc-swift), or `ChannelCredentials.secure()` (grpc-dart). Keep plaintext only for a local test server in debug builds.

**Verify:** Capture the app's gRPC traffic with a proxy and confirm it is a TLS handshake, not readable HTTP/2 frames.

**IDs:** MASWE-0026 · MASVS-NETWORK-1

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### XPL-018: Biometric check falls back to the device passcode

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours · **Only for:** banking, identity, health

**Why it matters:** When the prompt also accepts the device PIN or passcode, anyone who has watched the user unlock the phone can approve the action. For a payment or a vault unlock, that removes the point of the biometric.

**Fix:** For high-value actions, require `BIOMETRIC_STRONG` or `.biometryCurrentSet` with a key bound to it. Make the fallback a server-side step-up (password, passkey, or OTP), not the device PIN.

**Verify:** Trigger the sensitive action and confirm the prompt offers no "Use PIN" or "Enter Passcode" option.

**Other apps:** A device-passcode fallback is fine for unlocking an app that holds no high-value data.

**IDs:** MASWE-0021 · MASVS-AUTH-2 · MASTG-TEST-0326 · MASTG-TEST-0268 · MASTG-BEST-0031

**Read more:** [book §11.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/04-proving-who-is-calling.md#114-fallbacks-and-the-tension-inside-them)

### XPL-019: Private key or client certificate ships inside the app

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** days

**Why it matters:** Anything in the app package is public. A bundled private key, or a client-certificate keystore with its password in the code, lets anyone impersonate the app to your mTLS server or sign as you.

**Fix:** Remove the key and rotate it. For mTLS, have each device generate its key pair in the Keystore or Secure Enclave and enroll it with your server.

**Verify:** Unpack the release APK or IPA and search it for `PRIVATE KEY` and for `.p12`, `.pfx`, `.pem`, and `.key` files; nothing should be found.

**IDs:** MASWE-0003 · MASVS-STORAGE-1 · MASTG-TEST-0214

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-020: Zip entry name is used as a path without a containment check (Zip Slip)
